newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt court abolishes perpetual shop lease clause.
newsitem.headline: Egypt court abolishes perpetual shop lease clause.

text.p: Egypt's constitutional court has abolished a clause giving shop tenants the right to pass on the lease to their heirs, lawyers said on Wednesday.

Reactions to the Highest Constitutional Court ruling, issued in February, were mixed. Real estate owners said it restored their rights to end the lease or raise rents. Shop tenants say it is irresponsible and will hurt them economically.
Mohamed al-Ghamri, lawyer and director of the Egyptian Organisation for Human Rights' research centre, said the ruling could be socially explosive.
"Social disturbances could take place if the issue is not wisely handled," he told Reuters. "The court has put the government in a dilemma."
Egypt in its economic reform programme is trying to shed the policies of the 1960s socialist era.

The government, as part of liberalisation, had been trying for years to issue a new law replacing the one governing ties between real estate owners and tenants, which was based on strict rent control and perpetual leases.
The law discouraged investors from building, which resulted in housing and business space shortages and unaffordable rents.
The court ruling abolished a clause in a 1977 law. It came into force when it appeared in the official gazette this month.
The ruling for the first time in decades gives real estate owners recourse in the court to prevent leases from being automatically passed on to a tenant's heirs.
But some believe that the ruling is a political one. "In my opinion, the issue was arranged (between the court and the government)," Ghamri said.
Many tenants demanded that the status quo continue with gradual rent increases.
Many shops in Cairo's old city are occupied by heirs.
"If the owner tries to kick me out of my shop, I'll kill him," shop tenant Shehata Fahmi Khalil angrily told Reuters.
"A civil war will erupt" if the ruling is applied, said another, declining to mention his name. "How can we leave the place where we earn our bread," he added.
